sections.title: Understanding Coupling in Software Design
sections.content:
Coupling measures the **degree of interdependence** between software modules or classes.

Think of it like building with LEGO bricks versus building with concrete blocks cemented together. With LEGO (low coupling), you can swap pieces easily. With cemented blocks (high coupling), removing one piece breaks everything around it.

In Java applications, **tight coupling** happens when class A directly instantiates class B using the **new** keyword—A now knows B's exact implementation details, constructor parameters, and internal structure. **Loose coupling** happens when A depends only on an interface that B implements—A knows what B can do, but not how B does it. The **coupling level** determines how much effort it takes to change, test, or replace a component. High coupling creates **maintenance nightmares** because a single change ripples through dozens of classes. Low coupling creates **flexible systems** where you can swap implementations, mock dependencies in tests, and evolve components independently.

In Spring Boot, the framework itself promotes low coupling through **dependency injection**—you declare dependencies as interfaces, and Spring wires up concrete implementations at runtime.

sections.title: Tight Coupling vs Loose Coupling in Spring Boot
When to Apply Low Coupling Strategies
sections.content: Apply loose coupling whenever you're building components that might change independently. **Use dependency injection with interfaces** when writing service layers that interact with external systems—payment gateways, notification services, data repositories. If you hardcode a direct dependency on EmailService, switching to SMS notifications requires rewriting OrderService. With an interface, you just swap the implementation. **Apply interface-based design** when writing testable code—you can't mock a class that's instantiated with new inside another class, but you can easily mock an injected interface. **Introduce abstraction layers** when integrating third-party libraries—wrap them in your own interface so if the library changes or you switch vendors, only the wrapper changes, not your entire codebase. In a Spring Boot e-commerce app, your OrderController should depend on OrderService interface, not the concrete implementation, so you can swap in a caching version or a distributed version without touching the controller.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Thinking all dependencies are bad coupling**: Freshers often try to eliminate all dependencies, but that's impossible—classes must interact. The goal is controlling the type and degree of coupling, not eliminating it entirely. Having many dependencies on stable abstractions (interfaces) is fine.
- **Using new keyword in service classes**: Creating dependencies with new EmailService() inside a business method tightly couples your service to that exact implementation. You can't test it without sending real emails, and you can't switch to SMS without editing code. Always inject dependencies through constructors.
- **Creating one interface per class reflexively**: Some freshers think every class needs an interface, creating IOrderService with only one implementation OrderServiceImpl. This is premature abstraction. Create interfaces when you need decoupling or multiple implementations, not as a ritual.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Coupling**: the degree to which one class depends on another—low coupling is the goal for maintainable systems
**Tight coupling**: direct instantiation with new keyword creates hard dependencies on concrete classes that are difficult to change or test
**Loose coupling**: depending on interfaces or abstract classes allows implementations to vary without affecting dependent code
**Dependency injection**: the primary mechanism for achieving loose coupling in Spring Boot—framework wires dependencies at runtime
**Change propagation**: high coupling means changes cascade through multiple classes; low coupling isolates changes to single components
**Testability**: loosely coupled code is easily tested with mocks and stubs; tightly coupled code requires real dependencies even in unit tests
**Interface segregation**: depend on the smallest interface necessary—don't couple to a 20-method interface when you only use 2 methods

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd say coupling measures how much one class depends on another. It's about the strength of the connection between modules. In a Spring Boot app, tight coupling happens when you use the new keyword to create dependencies directly inside a class. For example, if OrderService creates an EmailNotifier object with new EmailNotifier, then OrderService is tightly coupled to that exact email implementation. If you need to switch to SMS notifications, you have to edit OrderService code. That's risky and makes testing hard because you can't mock that email service. Loose coupling is better. You define a NotificationService interface, and OrderService depends on that interface through constructor injection. Spring wires up the actual implementation at runtime. Now you can swap in different implementations—email, SMS, push notifications—without touching OrderService. You can also pass in a mock during testing. The key principle is program to interfaces, not implementations. One mistake freshers make is thinking coupling means any dependency at all. That's not it. Classes have to interact. The question is whether they depend on concrete implementations or on abstractions. Another mistake is creating objects with new inside service methods instead of injecting them. That locks you into one implementation and kills testability. In real projects, loose coupling through dependency injection is what lets you maintain and extend systems without breaking everything.

question: What is cohesion in software design?
title: Cohesion — what it is and why high cohesion is desirable
direct_answer: Cohesion measures how focused a class is—how closely related its methods and responsibilities are. High cohesion means everything in the class belongs together and serves one purpose. Low cohesion means the class is a grab-bag of unrelated things. High cohesion is the goal—it makes classes easier to understand, test, and maintain.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding cohesion as the internal measure of how well a class's responsibilities fit together.

interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect cohesion to the Single Responsibility Principle and explain that high cohesion naturally leads to smaller, focused classes.

sections.title: Understanding Cohesion in Class Design
sections.content:
Cohesion measures how **strongly related and focused** the responsibilities of a single class are. Imagine a kitchen drawer: a high-cohesion drawer contains only utensils—forks, spoons, knives—all serving the same purpose. A low-cohesion drawer is a junk drawer with batteries, scissors, receipts, and tape—unrelated items thrown together.

In Java, a **highly cohesive class** has methods and fields that work together toward a single, well-defined purpose. An **OrderProcessor** that validates orders, calculates totals, and saves to the database has high cohesion—everything relates to order processing. A **UtilityClass** with methods for date formatting, string manipulation, file I/O, and random number generation has low cohesion—it's a dumping ground for miscellaneous functions. High cohesion means the class has a **clear reason to exist** and a **single axis of change**. When requirements change, you know exactly which class to modify. Low cohesion creates **confusing classes** where half the methods have nothing to do with the other half. You spend time figuring out what the class actually does, and changes in one area unexpectedly break unrelated functionality. The **Single Responsibility Principle** from SOLID directly addresses cohesion: a class should have one reason to change. High cohesion is not about class size—a 500-line encryption class with all methods focused on cryptography has high cohesion.

emerald|Low|~grab-bag class|unrelated methods|a Util or Manager dump

sections.title: High Cohesion vs Low Cohesion in a Service Class
When to Focus on High Cohesion
sections.content:
Prioritize high cohesion when designing **service classes** in Spring Boot—each service should focus on one domain entity or business capability. UserService handles user operations, OrderService handles orders, PaymentService handles payments. Don't create a single ApplicationService that does everything.

Apply high cohesion in **repository interfaces**—a UserRepository should only have methods related to user persistence, not methods for logging, notifications, or unrelated entities. Keep **utility classes** cohesive by grouping only truly related functions—a DateUtils class should have date operations only, not string formatting or file I/O mixed in. In **controller classes**, keep each controller focused on one resource or aggregate—OrderController handles order endpoints, not user authentication or product catalog. If you find yourself adding a method that feels out of place, that's a signal cohesion is dropping. In a real e-commerce Spring Boot app, when you need to send an order confirmation email, don't add that method to OrderService—create a NotificationService. The notification logic doesn't belong with order processing logic.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Confusing cohesion with class size**: Freshers think high cohesion means small classes, but it's about focus, not line count. A 300-line SecurityService that handles authentication, authorization, and token management has high cohesion if all methods serve security. A 50-line HelperClass with random unrelated methods has low cohesion.
- **Creating God Classes**: Adding every new feature to an existing class because it's convenient. Your OrderService starts handling orders, then you add payment logic, then email notifications, then inventory management. Now it's a 2000-line monster with low cohesion. Each new responsibility should be a signal to extract a new class.
- **Misunderstanding utility classes**: Creating a Utils class and dumping every static method there. StringUtils, DateUtils, FileUtils all mixed into one ApplicationUtils. This destroys cohesion. Group related utilities together and keep them focused on one concern.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Cohesion**: measures how strongly related the responsibilities within a single class are—high cohesion means focused, low cohesion means scattered
**Single Responsibility Principle**: directly addresses cohesion by requiring each class to have one reason to change
**High cohesion benefits**: makes classes easier to understand, test, and maintain because all parts work together toward one purpose
**Low cohesion symptoms**: methods that don't relate to each other, fields used by only some methods, difficulty naming the class clearly
**Size is not cohesion**: a large class can have high cohesion if all code serves one focused purpose; a small class can have low cohesion if it does unrelated things
**God Class antipattern**: the extreme of low cohesion—one class that knows and does everything, making it fragile and hard to change
**Refactoring for cohesion**: when adding a new method feels awkward, extract a new class—don't force unrelated functionality into an existing class

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd explain that cohesion is about how focused a class is. It measures whether everything in the class belongs together or if it's a mix of unrelated stuff. High cohesion means all the methods and fields work together for one clear purpose. Low cohesion means the class is doing too many different things that don't really relate. For example, in a Spring Boot app, a UserService with methods like createUser, updateUser, and findById has high cohesion. All those methods are about user management. But if that same UserService also has methods for sending emails, generating reports, and processing payments, that's low cohesion. Those responsibilities don't belong together. The class becomes confusing and hard to maintain. High cohesion is directly connected to the Single Responsibility Principle. A class should have one reason to change. If your UserService changes because of user logic and also because of email template changes and also because of payment provider updates, that's three reasons to change, which means low cohesion. A common mistake freshers make is thinking cohesion is just about keeping classes small. It's not about size. A 500-line class that's entirely focused on complex encryption logic has high cohesion. A 50-line class with five unrelated utility methods has low cohesion. Another mistake is creating one big service class and adding every new feature to it because it's easy. That's how you end up with a God Class. In real projects, when I need to add functionality, I ask does this belong in the existing class or should it be a new class? If it feels forced, that's a sign cohesion would drop. High cohesion makes code predictable and easy to test.

beats.content: Interfaces reduce coupling by inserting an indirection layer. Instead of PaymentService depending directly on StripePayment, it depends on a PaymentGateway interface. StripePayment and PayPalPayment both implement the interface. PaymentService knows neither of them.
The result: swapping Stripe for PayPal means adding a new class that implements PaymentGateway and updating the Spring configuration. PaymentService is untouched. That's loose coupling in practice.

non-obvious: decoupling is also what makes unit tests fast. When PaymentService depends on an interface, tests inject a mock implementation. No real payment gateway is called. This daily testing benefit is worth emphasizing when you talk about loose coupling.

speakable_v2.cap: Interfaces decouple by hiding the implementation. You can swap, extend, or mock without touching the class that depends on the interface.

question: How do interfaces reduce coupling between classes?
title: Interfaces as a tool for reducing coupling in Java
direct_answer: Interfaces reduce coupling by introducing an indirection layer. Instead of class A directly depending on class B, A depends on interface I, and B implements I. A doesn't know B exists—it only knows the contract defined by I. You can swap B for any other implementation of I without touching A. This is the principle: program to interfaces, not implementations.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical understanding of how interfaces enable loose coupling in Java and Spring applications.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking interfaces are only useful when you have multiple implementations—missing that their primary value is decoupling and testability.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect interfaces to the Dependency Inversion Principle and explain how Spring uses them for dependency injection and proxy-based features like transactions.

sections.title: How Interfaces Enable Loose Coupling
sections.content:
Interfaces reduce coupling by creating an **abstraction layer** between classes. Instead of class A directly knowing about class B's implementation details, A only knows the **contract** defined by interface I, and B happens to implement that contract.

Think of it like using a power outlet: you plug in your laptop without knowing if the electricity comes from solar panels, coal, or nuclear—you only care about the **interface specification** (voltage, frequency).

In Java, when OrderService depends on the PaymentGateway interface instead of the concrete StripePaymentGateway class, OrderService has **no knowledge** of Stripe-specific code. You can swap in PayPalPaymentGateway or MockPaymentGateway without changing a single line in OrderService. This is the **Dependency Inversion Principle** from SOLID: high-level modules should depend on abstractions, not concrete implementations. The coupling is now between OrderService and the interface, which is a **stable contract** that rarely changes, not between OrderService and the volatile implementation details of a third-party payment library.

In Spring Boot, this pattern is fundamental: you inject dependencies as interfaces, and Spring wires up the concrete implementation at runtime. This enables **testability** because you can inject mock implementations during tests. It enables **flexibility** because you can change implementations through configuration without code changes. The interface acts as a **firewall**—changes inside the implementation don't propagate to dependent classes as long as the contract stays the same.

sections.title: Reducing Coupling with Interfaces in Spring Boot
When to Introduce Interfaces for Decoupling
sections.content:
Introduce interfaces when integrating **external systems**—payment gateways, email services, SMS providers, cloud storage. These are volatile dependencies that might change vendors or require mocking in tests. Define your own interface like PaymentService and wrap the third-party library in an implementation.

Use interfaces for **data access layers**—Spring Data JPA repositories are already interfaces, which is why you can easily swap database implementations or use in-memory databases for testing.

Apply interfaces when building **testable services**—if a service depends on another service, make that dependency an interface so you can inject mocks during unit tests. Don't create interfaces **prematurely**—if you have one service with no reason to vary, just use the concrete class. Interfaces add complexity and indirection, so only introduce them when you need the decoupling benefit. In a Spring Boot app, use interfaces for cross-layer dependencies—controller depends on service interface, service depends on repository interface—but within a single layer, direct dependencies on concrete classes are often fine. When you need to support multiple implementations like caching versus non-caching repository, that's when interfaces shine.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only creating interfaces when you have multiple implementations**: This misses the point. Interfaces provide decoupling and testability even with one implementation. If OrderService depends on PaymentGateway interface with only StripePaymentGateway implementation, you can still mock it in tests and swap implementations later without touching OrderService. The future flexibility and testability are the value.
- **Creating IService for every service reflexively**: Freshers learn interfaces reduce coupling and create IUserService with UserServiceImpl even when there's no variation, no mocking need, and no external dependency. This is cargo-cult programming—you're adding complexity without benefit. Use interfaces when you need decoupling, not as a ritual.
- **Fat interfaces**: Creating one NotificationService interface with twenty methods for emails, SMS, push notifications, logging, and audit trails. This creates tight coupling because any class depending on NotificationService must know about all twenty methods even if it uses one. Apply Interface Segregation Principle—create focused interfaces like EmailSender, SMSSender with only the methods needed.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Abstraction layer**: interfaces reduce coupling by creating a contract between classes without exposing implementation details
**Dependency Inversion Principle**: depend on abstractions like interfaces, not on concrete implementations—high-level modules shouldn't know low-level details
**Swappable implementations**: with interfaces, you can replace implementations without modifying dependent code—change payment providers without touching OrderService
**Testability**: interfaces enable mocking in unit tests—inject a fake implementation instead of requiring the real external system
**Spring Boot integration**: Spring's dependency injection relies on interfaces—you declare dependencies as interfaces and framework wires concrete implementations
**Stable contracts**: interfaces change rarely; implementations change frequently—depending on the interface shields you from implementation volatility
**Not always needed**: don't create interfaces reflexively—only introduce them when you need decoupling, multiple implementations, or testability benefits

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd say interfaces reduce coupling by creating a layer of abstraction between classes. Instead of class A directly depending on class B, A depends on interface I, and B implements I. Now A doesn't know anything about B's implementation—it only knows the contract defined by the interface. This lets you swap implementations without changing A. For example, in a Spring Boot app, if OrderService depends on the concrete class StripePaymentGateway, then OrderService knows all the Stripe-specific details. If you want to switch to PayPal, you have to modify OrderService code. But if OrderService depends on the PaymentGateway interface, and StripePaymentGateway implements that interface, then OrderService has no idea Stripe exists. It just calls the processPayment method on the interface. You can swap in PayPalPaymentGateway or a MockPaymentGateway for testing without touching OrderService. This is the Dependency Inversion Principle from SOLID—depend on abstractions, not concrete classes. The interface is a stable contract that doesn't change often, while implementations change all the time. Spring Boot uses this pattern everywhere. You inject dependencies as interfaces through constructors, and Spring wires up the actual implementation at runtime. This also makes testing easy because you can pass in a mock implementation that doesn't call real APIs. One common mistake freshers make is thinking interfaces are only useful when you have multiple implementations right now. That's wrong. Even with one implementation, interfaces give you testability and future flexibility. You can mock the interface in tests, and you can swap implementations later without code changes. Another mistake is creating an interface for every single class because someone said it's a best practice. That's overkill. Use interfaces when you're dealing with external dependencies, when you need testability, or when you expect variation. Don't create IUserService with UserServiceImpl if there's no benefit—you're just adding complexity. In real projects, interfaces let you isolate changes. If the payment provider changes their API, only the implementation class changes. The rest of your application is protected because it depends on your interface, not their API.

question: What is the relationship between coupling and cohesion?
title: Coupling and cohesion — the dual metrics of good design
direct_answer: The ideal design has high cohesion—each class is focused on one thing—and low coupling—classes depend on each other minimally through abstractions. They are complementary forces: highly cohesive classes naturally have fewer reasons to depend on other classes, which reduces coupling. The famous formula is high cohesion plus low coupling equals good design.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you understand the relationship between these two metrics and can articulate the design ideal.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating them as opposing forces or thinking you must sacrifice one for the other—they actually reinforce each other.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that improving cohesion often naturally reduces coupling because focused classes have fewer external dependencies.

sections.title: How Cohesion and Coupling Work Together
sections.content:
Cohesion and coupling are the **yin and yang of software design**—they measure different dimensions but work together to define code quality. **Cohesion** is internal: how focused is this class? **Coupling** is external: how much does this class depend on others? The design ideal is **high cohesion with low coupling**: each class has a clear, focused purpose and depends minimally on other classes through well-defined interfaces. These aren't opposing forces that you balance—they're **complementary forces** that reinforce each other. When you increase cohesion by splitting a God Class into focused services, coupling naturally decreases because each new class needs fewer external dependencies. A **UserService** that only handles user operations doesn't need to depend on PaymentGateway, EmailSender, and ReportGenerator like the original God Class did. Conversely, when you reduce coupling by introducing interfaces, you often identify misplaced responsibilities, which improves cohesion. The relationship is symbiotic: **well-designed systems exhibit both properties simultaneously**.

In Spring Boot applications, this manifests as focused service classes (high cohesion) that depend on each other through injected interfaces (low coupling). A poorly designed system has low cohesion (classes do too many things) and high coupling (classes know too much about each other's internals), creating a **fragile, unmaintainable mess**.

sections.title: Applying Cohesion and Coupling Together
sections.content:
Apply both principles when **refactoring legacy code**—split low-cohesion God Classes into focused services (improving cohesion), then introduce interfaces between them (reducing coupling).

Use both when **designing new features**—before writing code, identify the single responsibility (cohesion) and what abstractions it needs from other components (coupling). For example, adding a loyalty points feature: create a LoyaltyService (high cohesion) that depends on OrderService interface, not the concrete implementation (low coupling).

Apply in **code reviews**—ask two questions: Does this class have a clear, single purpose? Does it depend on concrete classes or abstractions? If a pull request adds payment logic to OrderService, that's a cohesion violation. If it instantiates PaymentGateway with new, that's a coupling violation. In Spring Boot project structure, organize packages by feature or domain (high cohesion within packages) and use dependency injection for cross-package dependencies (low coupling between packages). When you achieve both, you get systems that are easy to understand, test, and change.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating them as a trade-off**: Freshers often think you must sacrifice cohesion to get low coupling or vice versa. That's false. They work together—improving one usually improves the other. If you split a God Class (improving cohesion), you naturally reduce how many dependencies it needs (reducing coupling).
- **Focusing only on coupling**: Some developers learn about dependency injection and interfaces but ignore cohesion. They create loosely coupled classes that still have low cohesion—each class does five unrelated things but depends on abstractions. You need both. The interfaces reduce coupling, but the focused responsibilities create cohesion.
- **Creating trivial classes for the wrong reason**: Splitting a 100-line class into ten 10-line classes doesn't automatically improve cohesion or coupling. If those ten classes are still interdependent and unfocused, you've just made the problem worse. Split classes based on responsibility boundaries, not arbitrary size limits.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **Complementary forces**: cohesion and coupling work together, not against each other—high cohesion naturally reduces coupling
**Design ideal**: aim for high cohesion (focused classes) and low coupling (dependencies through abstractions) simultaneously
**Cohesion reduces coupling**: when you split a God Class into focused services, each new service needs fewer external dependencies
**Coupling reveals cohesion issues**: introducing interfaces often exposes misplaced responsibilities that should be extracted
**SOLID principles**: Single Responsibility (cohesion) and Dependency Inversion (coupling) are formalized versions of these concepts
**Refactoring synergy**: improving one metric often improves the other—split classes by responsibility, then inject dependencies via interfaces
**Not a trade-off**: you don't sacrifice cohesion to get low coupling or vice versa—good design achieves both together

sections.title: Code Example
How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: I'd say cohesion and coupling are two sides of the same coin. Cohesion is internal—it's about how focused a class is. Coupling is external—it's about how much classes depend on each other. The relationship is that they work together, not against each other. The ideal is high cohesion and low coupling at the same time. When you have highly cohesive classes, they naturally have lower coupling because a focused class doesn't need to depend on as many other things. For example, if I have a God Class that handles users, orders, payments, and notifications, it has low cohesion because it does too many unrelated things, and it has high coupling because it needs dependencies on user repositories, payment gateways, email services, and order databases all in one place. When I refactor that into separate UserService, OrderService, PaymentService, and NotificationService classes, each service now has high cohesion because it focuses on one thing. And they have low coupling because each service only depends on the specific interfaces it needs, not on everything. The key insight is that improving cohesion usually improves coupling too. If I split a class by responsibilities, the new classes each need fewer dependencies. A common mistake is thinking these are opposing forces that you have to balance. Freshers sometimes think if I make classes more cohesive, I'll increase coupling because now I have more classes talking to each other. But that's not how it works. Focused classes depend on fewer things, and you use interfaces to keep those dependencies loose. Another mistake is only worrying about one of them. You can have low coupling with dependency injection but still have God Classes with low cohesion. You need both. In a real Spring Boot app, this shows up as small, focused service classes that are injected into each other through interfaces. That's high cohesion plus low coupling working together.

question: What is a God Class and how does it violate cohesion and coupling?
title: God Class antipattern — low cohesion and high coupling
direct_answer: A God Class is a class that knows too much and does too much—it's the central hub of the entire application. It has low cohesion because it handles unrelated responsibilities, and it creates high coupling because every other class depends on it. Changing it is dangerous because one mistake breaks the whole system. It's the opposite of good design.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to identify and articulate a common antipattern that violates multiple design principles simultaneously.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Only saying God Class is too big without explaining the cohesion and coupling violations or connecting it to SOLID principles.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect God Class to violations of Single Responsibility Principle, low cohesion, high coupling, and explain how to refactor it into focused services.

sections.title: The God Class Antipattern
sections.content:
A **God Class** is the ultimate design antipattern—a single class that knows too much and does too much, acting as the central control point for the entire application.

Think of it as the **one ring to rule them all**: it handles user management, order processing, payments, notifications, logging, and database access all in one massive file. It's called a God Class because it has **godlike knowledge and power** over the system. This violates both cohesion and coupling catastrophically. **Low cohesion**: the class contains dozens of unrelated responsibilities—methods for user authentication sit next to methods for generating PDF reports sit next to methods for calculating tax. Nothing belongs together. **High coupling**: every other class in the system depends on this God Class because it owns all the important logic. To test anything, you must instantiate this monster with all its dependencies. To change anything, you risk breaking everything because the class is so interconnected internally. God Classes often start innocently—a small ApplicationService that handles a few things—but grow over time as developers keep adding just one more method because it's convenient. Eventually, you have a **2000-line monstrosity** that no single developer fully understands. It violates the **Single Responsibility Principle** spectacularly—it has twenty reasons to change, not one. Changes are risky because modifying one method can unexpectedly break another unrelated method through shared state.

sections.title: God Class Example and Refactoring
Identifying and Refactoring God Classes
sections.content:
Identify God Classes during **code reviews**—look for service classes over 500 lines, classes with more than ten public methods, or classes that import from every corner of the codebase. If the class name is generic like ApplicationService, Manager, or Utility, that's a red flag. When **adding new features**, if you keep modifying the same class regardless of what feature you're building, it's a God Class. Refactor by identifying **responsibility clusters**—group methods that operate on the same data or serve the same business purpose. Extract each cluster into a focused class: UserService, OrderService, NotificationService.

Use **dependency injection** to wire the new services together instead of having them all in one place.

Apply the **Single Responsibility Principle** as your guide: each extracted service should have one reason to change. In a Spring Boot e-commerce app, if your OrderController has methods for placing orders, managing inventory, sending emails, and generating reports, split it into OrderController, InventoryController, NotificationController, and ReportController. Each focused controller (high cohesion) depends on focused services (low coupling) through interfaces.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Only complaining about size**: Freshers say God Class is too big without explaining why size matters. The problem isn't line count—it's that the class has low cohesion and high coupling. A 2000-line class doing one complex thing well isn't a God Class. A 500-line class doing fifteen unrelated things is.
- **Not connecting to SOLID violations**: God Classes violate Single Responsibility Principle (multiple reasons to change), Open-Closed Principle (you must modify it for every new feature), and Dependency Inversion Principle (other classes depend on this concrete class, not abstractions). Explain these connections in interviews.
- **Creating micro God Classes**: After learning about God Classes, some developers split one 2000-line class into five 400-line classes that still do too many things each. You didn't fix the problem—you just distributed it. Each extracted class must have a single, focused responsibility. The refactoring isn't about hitting a line count target; it's about separating concerns.

sections.title: Key Points
content: **God Class**: antipattern where one class handles too many unrelated responsibilities, acting as the central hub of the application
**Low cohesion**: God Classes mix unrelated functionality—user logic, payment logic, email logic, reporting all in one class
**High coupling**: every other class depends on the God Class, making it impossible to change without risking widespread breakage
**Single Responsibility violation**: God Classes have multiple reasons to change, violating the most fundamental SOLID principle
**Evolutionary trap**: God Classes often start small but grow over time as developers add just one more method for convenience
**Refactoring strategy**: identify responsibility clusters and extract focused services, connecting them via dependency injection
**Testability nightmare**: testing any functionality requires instantiating the entire God Class with all its dependencies, making unit testing impractical

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: A God Class is the ultimate antipattern where one class tries to do everything. It's called a God Class because it has godlike knowledge and control over the entire application. It handles user management, orders, payments, notifications, logging—everything important lives in this one massive class. This violates both cohesion and coupling badly. For cohesion, the God Class has extremely low cohesion because it mixes unrelated responsibilities. Methods for authenticating users are next to methods for generating PDF reports next to methods for calculating shipping costs. Nothing is focused. For coupling, the God Class creates high coupling because every other class in the system depends on it. To test anything, you need to instantiate this monster with all its dependencies. To change anything, you risk breaking everything because the class is so tangled internally. God Classes also violate the Single Responsibility Principle completely. They don't have one reason to change—they have twenty reasons to change. If user logic needs an update, you modify this class. If tax calculation needs an update, you modify the same class. If email templates change, same class. That makes every change risky because you're touching code that affects unrelated features. A common mistake is just saying it's too big. Size isn't the real problem. A 2000-line encryption library with all methods focused on cryptography isn't a God Class. But a 500-line class doing ten unrelated things is. The real problem is low cohesion and high coupling together. To refactor a God Class, you identify clusters of related methods and extract them into focused services. If the God Class has user methods, order methods, and notification methods, you create UserService, OrderService, and NotificationService. Then you wire them together with dependency injection through interfaces. That gives you high cohesion in each service and low coupling between them. In real projects, God Classes usually start small but grow over time because it's convenient to keep adding methods to the existing class. You have to actively resist that temptation.
